Status: API · Header: R_ext/Memory.h · Protect: n/a · Errors: never · Since: — · R equivalent: gc


3.1.2 R_cycle_detected()
Detect a reference cycle between two objects.
Rboolean R_cycle_detected(SEXP s, SEXP child);
Status: non-API · Header: Defn.h · Protect: n/a · Errors: never · Since: — · R equivalent: —
You might wonder what all the PROTECT() calls do. They tell R that the object is in use and shouldn’t be deleted if the garbage collector is activated. (We don’t need to protect objects that R already knows we’re using, like function arguments.)
You also need to make sure that every protected object is unprotected. UNPROTECT() takes a single integer argument, n, and unprotects the last n objects that were protected. The number of protects and unprotects must match. If not, R will warn about a “stack imbalance in .Call”. Other specialised forms of protection are needed in some circumstances:

UNPROTECT_PTR() unprotects the object pointed to by the SEXP,
PROTECT_WITH_INDEX() saves an index of the protection location that can be used to replace the protected value using REPROTECT().

Consult the R externals section on garbage collection for more details.

text:
3.3 How PROTECT works
Objects protected by PROTECT() are placed on a protection stack (internally called R_PPStack), which itself is just an array of SEXPs. A protection index, called R_PPStackTop, denotes the top of the protection stack. When UNPROTECT()ing a (number) of objects, the stack top is decremented, and so all SEXPs ‘overflowing’ the R_PPStack are considered unprotected and hence eligible for garbage collection.
Note that this implies that PROTECT_WITH_INDEX() and REPROTECT() are merely APIs for modifying elements within the protection stack. UNPROTECT_PTR() performs a search (from the top of the stack) to find the element to unprotect.

3.4 Using PROTECT
Properly protecting the R objects you allocate is extremely important! Improper protection leads to difficulty diagnosing errors, typically segfaults, but other corruption is possible as well. In general, if you allocate a new R object, you must PROTECT it.

3.4.1 R_PreserveObject, R_ReleaseObject


3.4.2 R_PreserveObject() (R_ReleaseObject())
Preserve an object across C calls by adding it to R’s precious list.
void R_PreserveObject(SEXP);
void R_ReleaseObject(SEXP);
Status: API · Header: Rinternals.h · Protect: n/a · Errors: never · Since: — · R equivalent: —
The primary structure that R uses for protecting objects is the so-called R_PreciousList, which is just a pairlist of SEXPs; the R_PPStack protection stack is part of this list. These functions need to be used with care: because R_ReleaseObject() performs a recursive search for the object to release, inserting and later removing many SEXPs in the same order can cause performance regressions. See this dplyr issue for an interesting manifestation of this problem.
See also: PROTECT()

5.1.1 Rf_xlength() (Rf_length())
Get the length of a vector.
R_xlen_t Rf_xlength(SEXP x);
R_len_t Rf_length(SEXP x);
Status: API · Header: Rinternals.h · Protect: not needed · Errors: never · Since: — · R equivalent: length()

x: any vector.

Historically, R vectors were limited to length 2^31 - 1, and most vectors are still shorter than this, so the int-based Rf_length() interface suffices. As of R 3.0.0, vectors can have length up to 2^64 - 1; use the R_xlen_t-based Rf_xlength() if you want your code to be as general as possible. Also works on pairlists, where it is O(n).

As of R 3.0.0, R vectors can have length up to \(2 ^ {64} - 1\). If you want your code to be as general as possible, you should instead use the R_xlen_tbased interface:

6.1 Encodings
A character vector (STRSXP) is effectively an array of pointers to CHARSXPs, which are stored in a global string pool. This design allows individual CHARSXP’s to be shared between multiple character vectors, reducing memory usage.
Each CHARSXP has an encoding associated with it:

  CE_NATIVE = 0,
  CE_UTF8   = 1,
  CE_LATIN1 = 2,
  CE_BYTES  = 3,
  CE_SYMBOL = 5,
  CE_ANY    = 99
} cetype_t;

6.2 Creating from C strings

6.2.1 Rf_mkChar() (Rf_mkCharLen())
Create a CHARSXP from a C string in the current encoding.
SEXP Rf_mkChar(const char* x);
SEXP Rf_mkCharLen(const char* x, int n);
Status: API · Header: Rinternals.h · Protect: result · Errors: can throw · Since: — · R equivalent: —
Rf_mkChar() uses a null-terminated string; Rf_mkCharLen() uses a specified length. Typically these calls don’t need to be protected as they are immediately assigned into a STRSXP. These calls will crash R if passed a NULL; it is your responsibility to check for that and return the correct value (typically "" or NA_STRING).
See also: Rf_mkCharCE(), Rf_ScalarString()


6.2.2 Rf_mkCharCE() (Rf_mkCharLenCE())
Create a CHARSXP from a C string in a specified encoding.
SEXP Rf_mkCharCE(const char* x, cetype_t encoding);
SEXP Rf_mkCharLenCE(const char* x, int n, cetype_t encoding);
Status: API · Header: Rinternals.h · Protect: result · Errors: can throw · Since: — · R equivalent: —
Most modern C libraries encode strings as UTF-8. This means you should typically use Rf_mkCharCE() or Rf_mkCharLenCE(), and avoid the other string creation methods including Rf_mkString().
See also: cetype_t(), Rf_mkChar()

Create a length-1 STRSXP from a CHARSXP or C string.
SEXP Rf_ScalarString(SEXP);
SEXP Rf_mkString(const char*);
Status: API · Header: Rinternals.h · Protect: result · Errors: can throw · Since: — · R equivalent: —
Rf_ScalarString() makes a STRSXP from a CHARSXP; Rf_mkString() makes a STRSXP from a C string. Note that these calls will crash R if passed a NULL.
See also: Rf_mkChar()
(Typically these calls don’t need to be protected as they are immediately assigned into a STRSXP.)

6.3 Convert to C string
To access the underlying C-string stored in a CHARSXP, use CHAR():

6.3.1 CHAR() (R_CHAR())
Access the underlying C string stored in a CHARSXP.
const char* R_CHAR(SEXP x);
#define CHAR(x) R_CHAR(x)
Status: API · Header: Rinternals.h · Protect: not needed · Errors: never · Since: — · R equivalent: —
To match the other vector accessor functions (LOGICAL(), INTEGER(), …), this is typically called as CHAR().
See also: Rf_translateCharUTF8()


6.3.2 Rf_translateCharUTF8() (Rf_translateChar(), Rf_translateChar0())
Translate a CHARSXP to a C string in a specified encoding.
const char* Rf_translateChar(SEXP x);
const char* Rf_translateChar0(SEXP x);
const char* Rf_translateCharUTF8(SEXP x);
Status: API · Header: Rinternals.h · Protect: not needed · Errors: can throw · Since: — · R equivalent: —
Rf_translateChar() translates to the native encoding; Rf_translateChar0() returns the string as is if bytes, otherwise translates to native encoding; Rf_translateCharUTF8() translates to UTF-8. Most modern C APIs use UTF-8, so you almost always want Rf_translateCharUTF8(). If re-encoding is necessary, the char* will be allocated by R_alloc() and will be automatically freed at the end of the call to .C, .Call, or .External; if you want to save it across calls to C, make a copy.
See also: CHAR()
NB: To match the other vector accessor functions (LOGICAL(), INTEGER(), …), this is typically called as CHAR().
Three functions create const char* with the specified encoding.

...

... // one or more calls to Rf_translateChar(), Rf_translateCharUTF8(), etc.
vmaxset(vmax);
